english.notes:
(i) Practical Considerations - although there is a difference between 'wounding with intent...' and 'inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent...', both are charged under the same section. See notes in section 18.
(ii) An assault under this section may take one of four different forms:-
(1) wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm
(2) causing grievous bodily harm with intent to do so;
(3) maliciously wounding with intent to resist or prevent the lawful apprehension etc. of any person;
(4) maliciously causing grievous bodily harm with intent to resist or prevent the lawful apprehension etc. of any person
(iii) 'Intent to cause grievous bodily harm - proof is required that the defendant must either specifically intend to cause grievous bodily harm, or know that grievous bodily harm was a virtually certain consequence of his action. Factors which may indicate 'specific intent' include: a repeated or planned attack, prior threats, the deliberate selection of a weapon or adaptation of an article to cause injury (eg breaking a glass before an attack), using an offensive weapon.
(iv) Intent to resist/prevent arrest - proof is required that the wound/GBH was inflicted maliciously, i.e. some harm must have been either intended or foreseen, although not necessarily the specific type or gravity of injury suffered or inflicted (a person unforeseeably injures an officer whilst trying to escape - not this offence. But if he intended/foresaw that even some minor injury would result - there could be an offence). Where the malice/intent cannot be proved, consider section 20 of the Act. Where the level of injury does not meet these criteria, consider section 47 or section 39 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
(v) See Section 284 of the Sentencing Act 2020 regarding mandatory life sentences.
(vii) Where this offence is committed against an emergency worker this is an aggravating factor - see section 67 Sentencing Act 2020.
(viii) If the offence has a terrorist connection, the court treats this as an aggravating factor, the offence specified in Schedule 1 to the Sentencing Act 2020, see section 69 of that Act.
(ix) Consent to serious harm for sexual gratification that has been obtained from the victim is not a defence - see section 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021.
(ix) Extended jurisdiction - see section 72 Domestic Abuse Act 2021.
